tldr: Using reinforcement learning and a single RGB-D camera, the authors realized in-hand assembly on real hardware: simultaneously holding, manipulating, and mating two rigid objects within a single dexterous robot hand without any second arm or fixtures.
hero_caption: Cooperative in-hand manipulation of two parts using only one hand. A single unified framework accomplishes three assembly tasks with distinct geometries and tolerance requirements: capping a bottle, depressing a syringe, and capping a marker.
overview:
Humans can cap a pen with the hand holding it or push a bottle cap back into place by assigning distinct, coordinated roles to different fingers. In contrast, existing robot hand research has largely focused on reorienting a single object within the hand or relying on two arms and specialized fixtures for assembly. Holding two separate parts in one hand while precisely mating them has been extremely difficult due to finger interference, complex contact modes, and severe visual occlusion caused by the hand itself.

To tackle this, the authors propose a unified reinforcement learning (RL) framework in simulation to achieve fixture-free, single-hand assembly of two rigid parts. The system introduces a function-based auxiliary reward that delegates the thumb and index finger to fine manipulation while assigning the middle, ring, and pinky fingers to stable support. It also regularizes hand posture toward a single human reference pose snapshot. Combined with an occlusion-robust single-camera pose estimation pipeline and an RNN policy that processes historical observations, the policy achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

Experiments show that the policy successfully executes three distinct assembly tasks on real hardware—Bottle, Syringe, and Marker—and exhibits self-recovery capabilities against strong external disturbances. Comparative evaluations across four different robotic hands also reveal that in-hand assembly serves as an effective benchmark for evaluating the morphological dexterity of multi-fingered hands.
contributions: Formulated the in-hand assembly task—cooperatively manipulating and mating two objects within a single dexterous hand without fixtures or a second arm—and established it as a new benchmark for evaluating dexterity.

Constructed a unified reinforcement learning framework that pairs function-based auxiliary rewards for finger role assignment with initialization from a single human reference pose snapshot to solve diverse assembly tasks.

Achieved zero-shot sim-to-real transfer purely from simulation training, demonstrating robust assembly under severe visual occlusion and external disturbances using only a single RGB-D camera and joint angle history.

sections.heading: Can you cap a pen with one hand? Tackling human-level finger coordination
sections.summary: Human dexterity relies on fingers coordinating with distinct, independent roles. To elicit this capability in robots, this paper tackles in-hand assembly: a challenging task where two rigid parts are mated within a single hand without any fixture or second arm.
sections.details:
While animals can push or pull objects with their limbs, assigning different functional roles to individual fingers to accomplish fine manipulation is a hallmark of human dexterity. Examples include depressing a syringe plunger with one hand or capping a pen with the hand that holds it. However, most prior dexterous hand research has remained limited to simple, repetitive behaviors such as pick-and-place or in-hand reorientation of a single object.

This study focuses on in-hand assembly: supporting two rigid bodies simultaneously within a single dexterous hand, aligning them precisely, and mating them. This task is exceptionally challenging for three main reasons:

- Rich contact dynamics requiring precise force control: Four to five fingers must coordinate at the millimeter scale, making demonstration collection via teleoperation or kinesthetic teaching impractical.
- Diversity of geometries and mating mechanisms: Different target objects feature varied shapes and degrees of freedom, rendering manual, per-task controller design unscalable.
- Severe visual occlusion: Objects fit closely together within the palm, obscuring them from camera views and drastically increasing state estimation errors.

The authors developed a unified framework based on reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, utilizing function-based reward shaping and a human pose snapshot. Relying on proprioceptive history (joint angles) to compensate for visual errors under occlusion, they achieved the world's first fixture-free, in-hand two-part assembly on real robotic hardware.

sections.heading: How does this differ from traditional grasping and assembly research?
sections.summary: Reviewing dexterous grasping, single-object rotation, and traditional peg-in-hole setups with dual arms or parallel grippers highlights the unique novelty and difficulty of fixture-free, cooperative two-object manipulation in one hand.
sections.details:
To clarify the positioning of this work, the authors categorize related prior research into two main streams:

### Dexterous Manipulation with Multi-Fingered Hands
Much of multi-fingered hand research has focused on grasping. However, enveloping power grasps can often be replicated by low-degree-of-freedom grippers. While some studies hold multiple objects in one hand, they typically partition fingers into independent groups without coordinating the objects relative to each other. In-hand reorientation has also been widely studied, but it is confined to single objects. Meanwhile, methods imitating human demonstrations struggle with the embodiment gap between human and robot hands, making fine-contact policies difficult to acquire.

### Robotic Assembly
Assembly is a classic robotic challenge, epitomized by peg-in-hole insertion. While RL-based contact-rich insertion policies have advanced, virtually all of them rely on a parallel gripper holding one part while the other is mounted to a fixture or held by a second arm. Dexterous hand studies have largely been limited to disassembly (such as uncapping) or bimanual coordination.

In short, mating two objects within a single general-purpose multi-fingered hand without any mounting fixture or second arm represents an unexplored frontier for assessing true robotic dexterity.

sections.heading: A unified framework: Finger role division and snapshot initialization
sections.summary: Assembly is formulated as driving two parts toward a goal relative pose. The approach combines functional rewards dividing the fingers into manipulation and support groups, initialization from a human snapshot, and occlusion-resilient monocular tracking.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
The two rigid bodies assembled in the hand are defined as the held part $\mathcal{O}_h$ and the fixed part $\mathcal{O}_f$. The fingers of hand $\mathcal{H}$ are divided into two functional subsets:
- Held set $\mathcal{F}_h = \{	ext{Thumb, Index}\}$: Pinches $\mathcal{O}_h$ and carries out fine alignment and insertion.
- Fixed set $\mathcal{F}_f = \{	ext{Middle, Ring, Pinky}\}$: Cradles and supports $\mathcal{O}_f$, counteracting insertion forces while assisting fine adjustments.

### 3.2 Target Tasks
Three tasks are evaluated: capping a bottle (Bottle), inserting a syringe plunger (Syringe), and capping a marker pen (Marker). Each task features distinct object dimensions, clearance tolerances, and finger coordination demands.

### 3.3 Observation and Action Spaces
The observation vector is compact at 34 dimensions: the center-of-mass positions of both objects in the wrist frame (3D each), unit vectors along their symmetry z-axes (3D each), and measured joint angles $q_t$ (22D). Neither velocities nor contact force sensors are included. Wrist roll and pitch are appended for tasks involving wrist inclination. The action $a_t \in [-1, 1]^{22}$ specifies delta joint targets for a 15 Hz PD controller.
On the real robot, FoundationPose tracks 6D poses from a single RealSense D435 camera, which are then transformed to the wrist frame. To prevent the tracker from latching onto the hand surface during severe occlusion, a depth consistency gate discards pose updates when the discrepancy between predicted and measured depth exceeds 8 cm.

### 3.4 Reward Design: Goal Reaching and Functional Auxiliary Rewards
The reward consists of two main components:
1. Goal-reaching reward: Exponential rewards penalizing the relative local frame in-plane error $e_{xy}$, insertion axis error $e_z$, and axial orientation tilt error $e_{	heta}$.
2. Functional auxiliary rewards: A product of a pinch term $ho^{	ext{pinch}}$ measuring contact of $\mathcal{F}_h$ with $\mathcal{O}_h$, a grasp term $ho^{	ext{grasp}}$ measuring contact of $\mathcal{F}_f$ with $\mathcal{O}_f$, and a pose regularization term $ho^{	ext{pose}}$ penalizing deviations from an initial reference posture. This discourages uncoordinated finger motion and guides the hand toward functional role division.

### 3.5 Human Snapshot Initialization
Because both objects must be initialized inside one hand, the framework extracts a single static frame (snapshot) from a human demonstration video. This pose is geometrically retargeted to the robot hand with slightly open fingers, and the objects are placed inside. To resolve initial penetration artifacts, an episode begins with a settling phase where random small disturbance forces are applied in simulation for a few steps to let the objects settle naturally.

captions.F2: Dimensions and geometries of the three assembly tasks (Bottle, Syringe, Marker). Fine-grained goal-reaching rewards are computed from the relative spatial relationship between reference point $p_{\text{ref}}$ and goal point $p_{\text{goal}}$ for each task.
captions.F3: Initial state generation process from a single human snapshot image. The human hand pose is geometrically retargeted to robot joint angles, followed by simulation settling with small perturbation forces to generate diverse, penetration-free initial configurations.

sections.heading: Zero-shot sim-to-real success and the impact of hand morphology
sections.summary: Trained policies transfer zero-shot to hardware with high success rates. Comparative evaluations across different robot hands demonstrate how critical thumb opposition and having five fingers are for in-hand assembly.
sections.details:
### Hand Morphology Benchmark
The task was evaluated across four distinct robot hands: Sharpa Hand, Wuji Hand, Allegro Hand, and XHand. The anthropomorphic Sharpa and Wuji hands, which feature human-like degrees of freedom and ranges of motion, achieved top performance. The four-fingered Allegro Hand achieved XY-plane alignment but struggled with deep Z-axis insertion due to the absence of a pinky finger to cradle the base. The XHand, which has limited finger abduction/adduction, failed even at alignment. This shows that in-hand assembly serves as a demanding testbed for evaluating mechanical hand designs.

### Ablation Studies
Simulation ablations highlighted several critical insights:
- Removing vision (proprioception-only) causes a severe performance drop, as the policy cannot handle initial object misalignments.
- An LSTM with internal hidden states handles the partially observed Markov decision process (POMDP) significantly better than a history-stacked MLP (History-MLP).
- Removing the functional auxiliary reward or reference pose regularization leads to poor local optima, sharply degrading learning efficiency and success rates.

### Robustness to Estimation Errors
Because policies are trained with 1 cm standard deviation Gaussian noise, they maintain over 60% performance during testing even when subjected to 3 cm random noise or systematic offset errors. The policy appears to implicitly infer object states from joint angle history despite degraded vision.

### Real-Robot Experiments and Disturbance Recovery
On physical hardware, open-loop replay of successful simulation trajectories managed alignment in only 3 out of 20 trials, whereas the proposed closed-loop policy achieved high success rates through full insertion. Furthermore, when human experimenters introduced strong external disturbances—such as flicking the bottle cap out of alignment or pulling the syringe plunger backward—the policy dynamically adjusted finger contacts and successfully resumed assembly on its own.

captions.F4: Distribution of goal error across four robotic hands. Five-fingered, high-DoF Sharpa and Wuji hands cluster tightly near the origin (high accuracy), whereas the four-fingered Allegro Hand achieves shallow Z-axis insertion and the low-DoF XHand struggles with basic alignment.
captions.F5: Simulation ablation results. Models lacking visual observations, replacing the LSTM with an MLP, or omitting functional and reference pose rewards suffer major drops in cumulative reward, underscoring the necessity of each component.
captions.F7: Recovery behaviors under unexpected disturbances on real hardware. When a person intentionally tilts the bottle cap or pulls the inserted plunger out, the hand immediately readjusts finger contacts and resumes assembly.

sections.heading: Current limitations and future horizons: Tabletop grasping to diverse tasks
sections.summary: This method focuses strictly on assembly once parts are already held in the hand; picking up parts from a table and re-grasping them remains future work. Expanding to other mating modes like threading is also targeted.
sections.details:
While representing a significant step forward, the authors acknowledge clear limitations.

First, the scope is restricted to manipulation that begins with objects already resting in the hand. A complete practical pipeline must autonomously pick up multiple parts from a tabletop and orient them within the hand prior to assembly. Integrating this preliminary stage (multi-object grasping and initial reorientation) into a long-horizon pipeline is essential. At present, human assistance is sometimes needed to lightly steady parts until the policy establishes stable grasps.

Second, the evaluated tasks are restricted to three plug-in insertion tasks. Future work aims to expand into operations requiring more complex contact mechanics, such as threading screws or high-force friction fits.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A milestone in unlocking true multi-fingered dexterity
sections.summary: The authors realized in-hand assembly of two objects using a single hand without external fixtures or dual arms. Functional specialization of fingers and coordinated contact transitions are key to reproducing human-level dexterity in robots.
sections.details:
This paper proposed and demonstrated in-hand assembly: supporting and mating two rigid bodies simultaneously within a single dexterous hand without external fixtures or auxiliary arms.

Because this task demands complex contact-mode transitions and high-precision control, it serves as a powerful benchmark for evaluating robotic dexterity. By combining a lightweight functional reward design with human pose snapshot initialization, reinforcement learning policies achieved robust assembly across three real-world tasks.

The central takeaway of this work is that dexterous manipulation emerges not merely from high degrees of freedom, but from finger specialization paired with dense inter-finger coordination. This research provides a crucial foundation for advancing robotic hands toward human-level versatile dexterity.

sections.heading: Appendix: Simulation setup and real-world tracking stabilization details
sections.summary: Details on contact stabilization parameters in IsaacSim, torque relaxation control to prevent motor overheating, and filtering strategies that keep monocular tracking stable despite severe visual occlusion.
sections.details:
The appendix details essential engineering implementations for reproducibility and physical execution.

### Simulation Setup (IsaacSim)
To stably simulate contact-rich assembly, the authors employ signed distance field (SDF) collision detection with a Gauss-Seidel solver. The physics timestep is $1/120$ s, and 32 position iterations are assigned to the hand articulation system to preserve stability during multi-finger contact.

### Motor Overheating Prevention on Real Hardware
Joint angles on the physical Sharpa Hand are sampled at 500 Hz and downsampled to 15 Hz for the policy. Pinching two objects simultaneously can lead to mechanical jamming, causing excessive motor current draw, overheating, and hardware damage. To protect the hardware, a stall-relaxation loop monitors deviations between commanded and actual joint positions, slightly relaxing targets whenever a stall threshold is exceeded.

### Monocular Camera Tracking Stabilization
An ArUco marker mounted on the robot wrist bracket provides accurate extrinsic calibration at initialization. Object tracking is handled by FoundationPose, augmented with several safeguards to prevent tracker drift when fingers obscure objects: (1) discarding updates with depth inconsistencies exceeding 8 cm, (2) rejecting inter-frame position jumps over 6 cm, (3) applying exponential smoothing filters, and (4) re-initializing from object contours if tracking is lost for more than 15 frames. These mechanisms maintain continuous real-time control even under heavy occlusion.

takeaways: The primary advantage of multi-fingered robot hands is not enveloping grasps, but finger coordination that splits fingers into distinct supporting and fine manipulation roles.

In contact-rich multi-finger manipulation, constraining hand posture using a single static snapshot while letting goal-reaching RL rewards govern fine contact adjustments is far more effective than imitating full dynamic trajectories.
Even under severe visual occlusion by the hand, combining domain randomization with joint angle history (LSTM) allows policies to implicitly correct for visual errors through proprioception.
In-hand assembly serves as an effective benchmark for evaluating mechanical hand dexterity, including finger count, range of motion, and thumb opposition (abduction).
limitations: Both objects must be pre-placed in the hand at the start of the task; an autonomous end-to-end pipeline that picks up both parts from a table is not yet realized.
Rigid-body simulation does not fully capture soft, compliant fingertip patch contacts, causing pinch grasps to slip in simulation at near-horizontal orientations and hindering training.
Evaluated assembly tasks are limited to plug-in insertion; extending to threading or tight friction fits will require higher-fidelity contact physics modeling.
